tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

schema.name: Workflow
schema.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

1	---
2	name: write-bdd-scenarios
3	description: Discover and write high-quality Gherkin scenarios in features/*.feature and derive skipped Playwright component tests in src/*.ct.tsx from them, ready for outside-in TDD with red-green-step. Use when asked to specify, plan, or write the next feature, scenarios, acceptance criteria, or BDD tests.
4	---
5	
6	# Write BDD scenarios
7	
8	Turn a feature idea into a Gherkin spec and a matching set of skipped acceptance tests. Implementation is out of scope: hand off to `red-green-step`.
9	
10	The reasoning and sources behind each rule are in [references/sources.md](references/sources.md). Read it when a rule needs justifying or you are unsure how to apply one.
11	
12	## 1. Understand before writing
13	
14	BDD is a conversation first and a file second. Do not jump to scenarios.
15	
16	- Read `features/*.feature`, `src/*.ct.tsx` and `src/App.tsx` so the new work reuses the existing vocabulary and does not duplicate scenarios.
17	- State the story: "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [value]." If you cannot name the value, ask the user. A story with no value is a candidate to drop.
18	- Run an Example Mapping pass in text, then show it to the user before writing files:
19	  - **Rules**: the acceptance criteria, one line each.
20	  - **Examples**: concrete cases under each rule, using real values ("Coffee", "4.50"), not "valid input".
21	  - **Questions**: anything you cannot answer from the repo or the story.
22	- Probe each rule with Liz Keogh's two questions:
23	  - Context: is there another context in which the same event gives a different outcome? (empty list, zero, duplicates, whitespace, very large values, decimals)
24	  - Outcome: is there another outcome that matters? (what the form shows afterwards, what is kept, what is not changed)
25	- Ask the user about the open questions with `AskUserQuestion`. Do not invent business rules. Stories discovered along the way that are out of scope go in a "Not now" list, not in the feature.
26	- Too many rules or examples means the story is too big. Propose a split.
27	
28	## 2. Write the feature file
29	
30	Location and naming come from CLAUDE.md: `features/<kebab-case-feature>.feature`.
31	
32	Structure:
33	
34	- `Feature:` title, then the story in the three-line "As a / I want / So that" form.
35	- `Background:` only for context every scenario needs, at most 4 lines.
36	- `Rule:` blocks when a feature has several distinct business rules, each grouping the examples that illustrate it.
37	- `Scenario:` for each example. Use `Scenario Outline` with `Examples` only when rows differ by data alone and the same outcome shape holds.
38	
39	Rules for every scenario:
40	
41	1. **One behaviour per scenario.** One When, and Then steps that all describe the same outcome.
42	2. **3-5 steps.** Longer means it is testing more than one thing or leaking mechanics.
43	3. **Declarative, not imperative.** Describe what the user achieves, not keystrokes. Apply Cucumber's test: would the wording change if the UI changed? If yes, rewrite it. "When I add an expense named "Coffee" with amount "5"" beats three steps filling fields and clicking.
44	4. **Not too declarative either.** Keep the vocabulary the UI contract needs (the "Name" and "Amount" fields, the "Add" button, expense rows, error text) so a test can be derived. Where a precise UI fact is the behaviour itself, as with "the name field is empty", state it.
45	5. **Concrete values.** Use realistic data that makes the rule visible. Pick values on both sides of every boundary.
46	6. **Context, event, outcome.** Given is a state, When is one event, Then is an observable result. Never put an action in Then, never put an assertion in Given.
47	7. **Observable outcomes only.** Then steps describe what the user sees, not internal state, function calls or storage.
48	8. **Atomic steps.** No conjunction steps such as "Given I have a Coffee and a Groceries expense". Split into `And` steps.
49	9. **Titles state the rule.** "Cannot add an expense without a name", not "Test 3" or "Validation".
50	10. **Domain language.** Use the words the user would use. Reuse existing phrasing from `features/` so steps stay consistent. No technical terms such as "state", "component" or "DOM".
51	11. **Independent scenarios.** None may rely on another scenario having run.
52	12. **No coupled scenarios.** If one scenario is necessarily true whenever another one is, merge them or drop the weaker one. The `red-green-step` skill stops on this, so catch it here.
53	
54	Order scenarios from the walking skeleton outwards: the simplest end-to-end happy path first, then variations, then edge cases and errors. This order is the order of the TDD steps.
55	
56	## 3. Review before showing the user
57	
58	Check each scenario against the list below and fix failures silently:
59	
60	- Does it have a business reason to exist, not just a code path to cover?
61	- Could a non-programmer read it and say whether it is right?
62	- Is any step a UI mechanic that belongs in the test code instead?
63	- Does any pair of scenarios pass or fail together?
64	- Is there a missing context or outcome from the Keogh questions?
65	
66	Then present the feature file and the list of open questions or "Not now" items. Wait for the user's approval before deriving tests.
67	
68	## 4. Derive the acceptance tests
69	
70	After approval, write one Playwright component test per scenario. Follow the "Playwright component tests" section of CLAUDE.md exactly (file naming, locators, timeouts, one test per Scenario or Examples row). In addition:
71	
72	- Mount `<App />` and drive only the public surface: labels, roles and visible text. No component internals, no mocks of the app's own code.
73	- Name each test after its scenario title, in plain words.
74	- Put the three Gherkin phases in the test body in order, with a blank line before the assertion: setup, action, assertion. Do not add comments.
75	- Extract the existing small helpers (field locators, `addExpense`, `expectExpenseRow`) and add new ones for new domain phrases, so a test reads like its scenario. Reuse helpers that already exist in the file.
76	- Each test builds its own data inline. Share nothing mutable between tests.
77	- Write every new test as `test.skip(`. The only exception is when the user says to start with the first one.
78	- Run `npx tsc -b` and `npm run lint`. The tests must compile and mount. Running `npm run test:ct` needs the sandbox disabled, see `red-green-step`.
79	
80	## 5. Hand off to outside-in TDD
81	
82	Finish by reporting:
83	
84	- the scenarios written, grouped by rule, in implementation order
85	- the open questions and "Not now" items
86	- the first test to drive, which should be the walking-skeleton scenario
87	
88	Before any implementation, suggest an independent review of the result with the `bdd-reviewer` agent (skill `review-bdd-scenarios`). Fix its blocking findings first.
89	
90	Then suggest running `red-green-step`, or the `red-green-implementer` agent, one scenario at a time. Do not write production code in this skill. A scenario must fail for a missing behaviour before anyone implements it.
91	
92	## Anti-patterns to refuse
93	
94	- Scenarios written from the code instead of from the user's goal.
95	- Test-per-function or test-per-branch scenarios.
96	- Imperative click-by-click scenarios.
97	- Scenarios asserting implementation details (CSS classes, state, storage).
98	- A huge Background.
99	- Scenario Outlines whose rows exercise different rules.
100	- Writing tests before the user has seen the scenarios.

---
name: write-bdd-scenarios
description: Discover and write high-quality Gherkin scenarios in features/*.feature and derive skipped Playwright component tests in src/*.ct.tsx from them, ready for outside-in TDD with red-green-step. Use when asked to specify, plan, or write the next feature, scenarios, acceptance criteria, or BDD tests.
---

# Write BDD scenarios

Turn a feature idea into a Gherkin spec and a matching set of skipped acceptance tests. Implementation is out of scope: hand off to `red-green-step`.

The reasoning and sources behind each rule are in [references/sources.md](references/sources.md). Read it when a rule needs justifying or you are unsure how to apply one.

## 1. Understand before writing

BDD is a conversation first and a file second. Do not jump to scenarios.

- Read `features/*.feature`, `src/*.ct.tsx` and `src/App.tsx` so the new work reuses the existing vocabulary and does not duplicate scenarios.
- State the story: "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [value]." If you cannot name the value, ask the user. A story with no value is a candidate to drop.
- Run an Example Mapping pass in text, then show it to the user before writing files:
  - **Rules**: the acceptance criteria, one line each.
  - **Examples**: concrete cases under each rule, using real values ("Coffee", "4.50"), not "valid input".
  - **Questions**: anything you cannot answer from the repo or the story.
- Probe each rule with Liz Keogh's two questions:
  - Context: is there another context in which the same event gives a different outcome? (empty list, zero, duplicates, whitespace, very large values, decimals)
  - Outcome: is there another outcome that matters? (what the form shows afterwards, what is kept, what is not changed)
- Ask the user about the open questions with `AskUserQuestion`. Do not invent business rules. Stories discovered along the way that are out of scope go in a "Not now" list, not in the feature.
- Too many rules or examples means the story is too big. Propose a split.

## 2. Write the feature file

Location and naming come from CLAUDE.md: `features/<kebab-case-feature>.feature`.

Structure:

- `Feature:` title, then the story in the three-line "As a / I want / So that" form.
- `Background:` only for context every scenario needs, at most 4 lines.
- `Rule:` blocks when a feature has several distinct business rules, each grouping the examples that illustrate it.
- `Scenario:` for each example. Use `Scenario Outline` with `Examples` only when rows differ by data alone and the same outcome shape holds.

Rules for every scenario:

1. **One behaviour per scenario.** One When, and Then steps that all describe the same outcome.
2. **3-5 steps.** Longer means it is testing more than one thing or leaking mechanics.
3. **Declarative, not imperative.** Describe what the user achieves, not keystrokes. Apply Cucumber's test: would the wording change if the UI changed? If yes, rewrite it. "When I add an expense named "Coffee" with amount "5"" beats three steps filling fields and clicking.
4. **Not too declarative either.** Keep the vocabulary the UI contract needs (the "Name" and "Amount" fields, the "Add" button, expense rows, error text) so a test can be derived. Where a precise UI fact is the behaviour itself, as with "the name field is empty", state it.
5. **Concrete values.** Use realistic data that makes the rule visible. Pick values on both sides of every boundary.
6. **Context, event, outcome.** Given is a state, When is one event, Then is an observable result. Never put an action in Then, never put an assertion in Given.
7. **Observable outcomes only.** Then steps describe what the user sees, not internal state, function calls or storage.
8. **Atomic steps.** No conjunction steps such as "Given I have a Coffee and a Groceries expense". Split into `And` steps.
9. **Titles state the rule.** "Cannot add an expense without a name", not "Test 3" or "Validation".
10. **Domain language.** Use the words the user would use. Reuse existing phrasing from `features/` so steps stay consistent. No technical terms such as "state", "component" or "DOM".
11. **Independent scenarios.** None may rely on another scenario having run.
12. **No coupled scenarios.** If one scenario is necessarily true whenever another one is, merge them or drop the weaker one. The `red-green-step` skill stops on this, so catch it here.

Order scenarios from the walking skeleton outwards: the simplest end-to-end happy path first, then variations, then edge cases and errors. This order is the order of the TDD steps.

## 3. Review before showing the user

Check each scenario against the list below and fix failures silently:

- Does it have a business reason to exist, not just a code path to cover?
- Could a non-programmer read it and say whether it is right?
- Is any step a UI mechanic that belongs in the test code instead?
- Does any pair of scenarios pass or fail together?
- Is there a missing context or outcome from the Keogh questions?

Then present the feature file and the list of open questions or "Not now" items. Wait for the user's approval before deriving tests.

## 4. Derive the acceptance tests

After approval, write one Playwright component test per scenario. Follow the "Playwright component tests" section of CLAUDE.md exactly (file naming, locators, timeouts, one test per Scenario or Examples row). In addition:

- Mount `<App />` and drive only the public surface: labels, roles and visible text. No component internals, no mocks of the app's own code.
- Name each test after its scenario title, in plain words.
- Put the three Gherkin phases in the test body in order, with a blank line before the assertion: setup, action, assertion. Do not add comments.
- Extract the existing small helpers (field locators, `addExpense`, `expectExpenseRow`) and add new ones for new domain phrases, so a test reads like its scenario. Reuse helpers that already exist in the file.
- Each test builds its own data inline. Share nothing mutable between tests.
- Write every new test as `test.skip(`. The only exception is when the user says to start with the first one.
- Run `npx tsc -b` and `npm run lint`. The tests must compile and mount. Running `npm run test:ct` needs the sandbox disabled, see `red-green-step`.

## 5. Hand off to outside-in TDD

Finish by reporting:

- the scenarios written, grouped by rule, in implementation order
- the open questions and "Not now" items
- the first test to drive, which should be the walking-skeleton scenario

Before any implementation, suggest an independent review of the result with the `bdd-reviewer` agent (skill `review-bdd-scenarios`). Fix its blocking findings first.

Then suggest running `red-green-step`, or the `red-green-implementer` agent, one scenario at a time. Do not write production code in this skill. A scenario must fail for a missing behaviour before anyone implements it.

## Anti-patterns to refuse

- Scenarios written from the code instead of from the user's goal.
- Test-per-function or test-per-branch scenarios.
- Imperative click-by-click scenarios.
- Scenarios asserting implementation details (CSS classes, state, storage).
- A huge Background.
- Scenario Outlines whose rows exercise different rules.
- Writing tests before the user has seen the scenarios.

---
name: write-bdd-scenarios
description: Discover and write Gherkin scenarios for apps/user-ui in apps/user-ui/features/<area>.feature and derive Vitest + Testing Library characterisation tests from them, following docs/1-refactoring-1-user-ui-refactoring-plan.md. Use when asked to specify, pin, or write scenarios, acceptance criteria, characterisation tests or BDD tests for the user UI.
---

# Write BDD scenarios (user-ui characterisation framework)

Turn an area of observable `apps/user-ui` behaviour into a Gherkin spec and a matching Vitest suite that mounts the real `<App />`. The framework is defined in `docs/1-refactoring-1-user-ui-refactoring-plan.md` (section 1). Read it first and follow it; this skill does not redefine it.

Two modes:

- **Characterisation (default while the App.tsx refactor is in progress).** Scenarios describe what the app does today. Tests pass as soon as they are written. Mutation testing, not RED-first, proves they would catch a break. This is the deliberate exception to the TDD rule named in the plan.
- **New behaviour.** Scenarios describe something the app does not do yet. Write the tests as `it.skip(` and hand them to TDD one at a time (RED, GREEN, REFACTOR).

Ask the user which mode applies if the request does not say. Production code is out of scope in both modes.

The reasoning behind each rule is in [references/sources.md](references/sources.md).

## 1. Understand before writing

BDD is a conversation first and a file second. Do not jump to scenarios.

- Read the plan's "Behaviours to pin" list, the existing `apps/user-ui/features/*.feature` and `apps/user-ui/src/**/*.test.tsx`, so new work reuses existing vocabulary and helpers and does not duplicate scenarios.
- Read the code that implements the area (`apps/user-ui/src/App.tsx` and its neighbours) and `docs/SPEC.md`. In characterisation mode the code is the source of truth for the outcome, but the scenario is still worded from the user's goal ("As an operator, I want unread badges so that I see which channels need me"), not from the code path.
- State the story: "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [value]." If you cannot name the value, ask the user.
- Run an Example Mapping pass in text and show it to the user before writing files:
  - **Rules**: one line each.
  - **Examples**: concrete cases per rule with real values ("#general", "Direct: alice, bob", "Load previous messages"), not "valid input".
  - **Questions**: anything you cannot answer from the repo.
- Probe each rule with Liz Keogh's two questions:
  - Context: is there another context in which the same event gives a different outcome? (archived, read-only, private vs public vs team-shared, offline agent, WebSocket down)
  - Outcome: is there another outcome that matters? (what is shown, kept or hidden afterwards, and which request the app sends)
- Ask the user the open questions with `AskUserQuestion`. Do not invent business rules.
- **Quirks.** In characterisation mode, when the code does something that looks wrong, pin it as it is and log it in a "Quirks" list. Do not fix it and do not silently skip it. Example from the plan: `DIRECT_GROUP` and `AGENT_AGENT_DM` channels pass the visibility rule but match no sidebar group, so they are never listed. Mark the scenario title or a tag (`@quirk`) so it is easy to find for the separate fix ticket.
- Out-of-scope stories go in a "Not now" list.
- Too many rules or examples means the area is too big. Propose a split. Areas follow the plan: auth, workspace load, sidebar, timeline, loading, composer, dialogs and management. One feature file and one test file per area.

## 2. Write the feature file

Location: `apps/user-ui/features/<area-kebab-case>.feature`.

Structure:

- `Feature:` title, then the story in three lines ("As a / I want / So that").
- `Background:` only for context every scenario needs, at most 4 lines.
- `Rule:` blocks for distinct business rules, each grouping its examples.
- `Scenario:` per example. `Scenario Outline` with `Examples` only when rows differ by data alone and the outcome shape holds (for example the visibility rule across channel kinds).

Rules for every scenario:

1. **One behaviour per scenario.** One When; all Thens describe the same outcome.
2. **3-5 steps.**
3. **Declarative, not imperative.** Describe what the operator achieves, not keystrokes. Would the wording change if the markup changed? If yes, rewrite it.
4. **Not too declarative.** Keep vocabulary the test needs to locate things: visible labels, button names, roles, visible text. Where a precise UI fact is the behaviour ("the send button is disabled"), state it.
5. **Concrete values** on both sides of each boundary (7 vs 8 password characters, one channel vs none).
6. **Context, event, outcome.** Given is state, When is one event, Then is an observable result. No action in Then, no assertion in Given.
7. **Observable outcomes only.** Two kinds are observable here: what the operator sees, and the HTTP requests the app sends (method, URL, body), since that is the app's real contract with the API. Never internal state, hooks, module calls or storage.
8. **Atomic steps.** No conjunction steps; split into `And`.
9. **Titles state the rule.** "Sign-in shows an error for wrong credentials", not "Test 3".
10. **Domain language.** The words an operator uses. No "state", "component", "DOM", "reducer".
11. **Independent scenarios.**
12. **No coupled scenarios.** If one is necessarily true whenever another is, merge or drop the weaker one.
13. **Time and transport are Given steps.** "Given the realtime connection is down", "When 10 seconds pass". Fake timers make these free; they must still be visible in the scenario.

Order from the walking skeleton outwards: simplest happy path first, then variations, then edge cases and errors.

## 3. Review before showing the user

Fix failures silently:

- Business reason to exist, not just a branch to cover?
- Readable by a non-programmer?
- Any step that is a UI mechanic belonging in the test helpers?
- Any pair of scenarios that pass or fail together?
- Missing context or outcome from the Keogh questions?
- Does it assert markup (class names, `aria-*` strings, layout)? Remove it. The plan treats those as implementation detail.

Present the feature file, the Quirks list and the open questions or "Not now" items. Wait for approval before deriving tests.

## 4. Derive the tests

After approval, write one test per Scenario (or per Examples row) in `apps/user-ui/src/characterisation/<area>.test.tsx`, following the plan's approach exactly:

**Stack**

- Vitest with `happy-dom` (switch a single file to `jsdom` only if a behaviour needs it), Testing Library. `fireEvent` for plain state changes; `user-event` only where realistic typing matters (Enter vs Shift+Enter, IME composition).
- Mount the real `<App />`. Fake only the outside world: a hand-rolled `fetch` stub with a route table, a fake `WebSocket` class the test can push events through, and the browser APIs (`history`/`location`, `clipboard`, `window.confirm`, `requestAnimationFrame`, fake timers). Stub `scrollHeight` and similar layout properties where needed and accept partial coverage there.
- Use the shared test harness (fetch stub, fake WebSocket, `renderApp`) from the support module in `apps/user-ui/src/characterisation/`. Reuse it. If it does not exist yet, create it as the first commit of step 0a before any scenario.

**What tests may import**

- Only `App`, types from `types.ts`, the harness, and factory functions (`getMockChannel`, `getMockEvent`, ...). Never import or mock `api.ts`, `config.ts` or any other internal module, or moving them would force test edits.
- Factories return complete objects with `Partial<T>` overrides. Keep fixtures small (for example 3 channels). No `let`, no `beforeEach`. Each test builds its own data and renders a fresh `App`.

**Test body**

- Name each test after its scenario title, in plain words.
- Three phases in order: setup, action, assertion, with a blank line before the assertion. No comments.
- Assert on visible text and roles, and on recorded requests (method, URL, body). Do not assert on class names or `aria-*` strings.
- Extract helpers for domain phrases ("signInAs", "openChannel", "receiveEvent") so a test reads like its scenario. Reuse existing ones.

**Time**

- Fake timers everywhere. Advance the fake clock and flush promises. No real `waitFor` timeouts.

**Speed budget**

- Whole suite under about 10 seconds, any single test under about 200ms. After writing a suite, run `npx vitest run apps/user-ui --reporter=verbose` and fix anything over budget immediately.

**Modes**

- Characterisation: tests are active and must be green. A new test that passes first time is expected; confirm it can fail by temporarily breaking the behaviour in a scratch edit, or leave that check to the Stryker pass.
- New behaviour: write every test as `it.skip(`.

**Checks**

- `npm run lint` and `npm test`. Both must stay green. Do not edit `App.tsx` while writing characterisation tests (plan step 0).

## 5. Mutation check and hand-off

For characterisation mode, finish by reporting:

- the scenarios written, grouped by rule
- the Quirks pinned, for separate fix tickets
- the open questions and "Not now" items
- suite timing against the budget

Then follow the plan's step 0c: run Stryker (vitest runner, scope `apps/user-ui/src/**`, excluding tests and `styles.css`, per-test coverage, incremental) on the extracted modules, not all of `App.tsx` at once. Add a test for each surviving mutant that is a real gap in conditionals, string literals or arithmetic. Ignore survivors in class names, `aria-*` strings and style code. Target about 80% on logic modules. Stryker support for the repo's vitest version is unverified; the plan's fallback is a hand-picked list of manual mutations.

For new-behaviour mode, suggest implementing one scenario at a time with outside-in TDD, starting with the walking-skeleton scenario.

Suggest an independent review with the `bdd-reviewer` agent (skill `review-bdd-scenarios`) before implementation or refactoring starts, if those exist in this repo.

## Anti-patterns to refuse

- Scenarios written from the code structure instead of the operator's goal.
- Test-per-function or test-per-branch scenarios.
- Imperative click-by-click scenarios.
- Assertions on markup, CSS classes, `aria-*` strings, component state or storage.
- Tests that import or mock `api.ts`, `config.ts` or other internals.
- `let`/`beforeEach` shared state; real timers; real network.
- Fixing a quirk inside a characterisation suite.
- A huge Background, or Scenario Outlines whose rows exercise different rules.
- Writing tests before the user has seen the scenarios.

# Write BDD scenarios (user-ui characterisation framework)

Turn an area of observable `apps/user-ui` behaviour into a Gherkin spec and a matching Vitest suite that mounts the real `<App />`. The framework is defined in `docs/1-refactoring-1-user-ui-refactoring-plan.md` (section 1). Read it first and follow it; this skill does not redefine it.

Two modes:

- **Characterisation (default while the App.tsx refactor is in progress).** Scenarios describe what the app does today. Tests pass as soon as they are written. Mutation testing, not RED-first, proves they would catch a break. This is the deliberate exception to the TDD rule named in the plan.
- **New behaviour.** Scenarios describe something the app does not do yet. Write the tests as `it.skip(` and hand them to TDD one at a time (RED, GREEN, REFACTOR).

Ask the user which mode applies if the request does not say. Production code is out of scope in both modes.

The reasoning behind each rule is in [references/sources.md](references/sources.md).

## 1. Understand before writing

BDD is a conversation first and a file second. Do not jump to scenarios.

- Read the plan's "Behaviours to pin" list, the existing `apps/user-ui/features/*.feature` and `apps/user-ui/src/**/*.test.tsx`, so new work reuses existing vocabulary and helpers and does not duplicate scenarios.
- Read the code that implements the area (`apps/user-ui/src/App.tsx` and its neighbours) and `docs/SPEC.md`. In characterisation mode the code is the source of truth for the outcome, but the scenario is still worded from the user's goal ("As an operator, I want unread badges so that I see which channels need me"), not from the code path.
- State the story: "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [value]." If you cannot name the value, ask the user.
- Run an Example Mapping pass in text and show it to the user before writing files:
  - **Rules**: one line each.
  - **Examples**: concrete cases per rule with real values ("#general", "Direct: alice, bob", "Load previous messages"), not "valid input".
  - **Questions**: anything you cannot answer from the repo.
- Probe each rule with Liz Keogh's two questions:
  - Context: is there another context in which the same event gives a different outcome? (archived, read-only, private vs public vs team-shared, offline agent, WebSocket down)
  - Outcome: is there another outcome that matters? (what is shown, kept or hidden afterwards, and which request the app sends)
- Ask the user the open questions with `AskUserQuestion`. Do not invent business rules.
- **Quirks.** In characterisation mode, when the code does something that looks wrong, pin it as it is and log it in a "Quirks" list. Do not fix it and do not silently skip it. Example from the plan: `DIRECT_GROUP` and `AGENT_AGENT_DM` channels pass the visibility rule but match no sidebar group, so they are never listed. Mark the scenario title or a tag (`@quirk`) so it is easy to find for the separate fix ticket.
- Out-of-scope stories go in a "Not now" list.
- Too many rules or examples means the area is too big. Propose a split. Areas follow the plan: auth, workspace load, sidebar, timeline, loading, composer, dialogs and management. One feature file and one test file per area.

## 2. Write the feature file

Location: `apps/user-ui/features/<area-kebab-case>.feature`.

Structure:

- `Feature:` title, then the story in three lines ("As a / I want / So that").
- `Background:` only for context every scenario needs, at most 4 lines.
- `Rule:` blocks for distinct business rules, each grouping its examples.
- `Scenario:` per example. `Scenario Outline` with `Examples` only when rows differ by data alone and the outcome shape holds (for example the visibility rule across channel kinds).

Rules for every scenario:

1. **One behaviour per scenario.** One When; all Thens describe the same outcome.
2. **3-5 steps.**
3. **Declarative, not imperative.** Describe what the operator achieves, not keystrokes. Would the wording change if the markup changed? If yes, rewrite it.
4. **Not too declarative.** Keep vocabulary the test needs to locate things: visible labels, button names, roles, visible text. Where a precise UI fact is the behaviour ("the send button is disabled"), state it.
5. **Concrete values** on both sides of each boundary (7 vs 8 password characters, one channel vs none).
6. **Context, event, outcome.** Given is state, When is one event, Then is an observable result. No action in Then, no assertion in Given.
7. **Observable outcomes only.** Two kinds are observable here: what the operator sees, and the HTTP requests the app sends (method, URL, body), since that is the app's real contract with the API. Never internal state, hooks, module calls or storage.
8. **Atomic steps.** No conjunction steps; split into `And`.
9. **Titles state the rule.** "Sign-in shows an error for wrong credentials", not "Test 3".
10. **Domain language.** The words an operator uses. No "state", "component", "DOM", "reducer".
11. **Independent scenarios.**
12. **No coupled scenarios.** If one is necessarily true whenever another is, merge or drop the weaker one.
13. **Time and transport are Given steps.** "Given the realtime connection is down", "When 10 seconds pass". Fake timers make these free; they must still be visible in the scenario.

Order from the walking skeleton outwards: simplest happy path first, then variations, then edge cases and errors.

## 3. Review before showing the user

Fix failures silently:

- Business reason to exist, not just a branch to cover?
- Readable by a non-programmer?
- Any step that is a UI mechanic belonging in the test helpers?
- Any pair of scenarios that pass or fail together?
- Missing context or outcome from the Keogh questions?
- Does it assert markup (class names, `aria-*` strings, layout)? Remove it. The plan treats those as implementation detail.

Present the feature file, the Quirks list and the open questions or "Not now" items. Wait for approval before deriving tests.

## 4. Derive the tests

After approval, write one test per Scenario (or per Examples row) in `apps/user-ui/src/characterisation/<area>.test.tsx`, following the plan's approach exactly:

**Stack**

- Vitest with `happy-dom` (switch a single file to `jsdom` only if a behaviour needs it), Testing Library. `fireEvent` for plain state changes; `user-event` only where realistic typing matters (Enter vs Shift+Enter, IME composition).

Stub `scrollHeight` and similar layout properties where needed and accept partial coverage there.

**What tests may import**

- Only `App`, types from `types.ts`, the harness, and factory functions (`getMockChannel`, `getMockEvent`, ...). Never import or mock `api.ts`, `config.ts` or any other internal module, or moving them would force test edits.
- Factories return complete objects with `Partial<T>` overrides. Keep fixtures small (for example 3 channels). No `let`, no `beforeEach`. Each test builds its own data and renders a fresh `App`.

- Name each test after its scenario title, in plain words.

- Assert on visible text and roles, and on recorded requests (method, URL, body). Do not assert on class names or `aria-*` strings.
- Extract helpers for domain phrases ("signInAs", "openChannel", "receiveEvent") so a test reads like its scenario. Reuse existing ones.

- Fake timers everywhere. Advance the fake clock and flush promises. No real `waitFor` timeouts.

**Speed budget**

- Whole suite under about 10 seconds, any single test under about 200ms. After writing a suite, run `npx vitest run apps/user-ui --reporter=verbose` and fix anything over budget immediately.

- Characterisation: tests are active and must be green. A new test that passes first time is expected; confirm it can fail by temporarily breaking the behaviour in a scratch edit, or leave that check to the Stryker pass.

## 5. Mutation check and hand-off

- the scenarios written, grouped by rule
- the Quirks pinned, for separate fix tickets
- the open questions and "Not now" items
- suite timing against the budget

Then follow the plan's step 0c: run Stryker (vitest runner, scope `apps/user-ui/src/**`, excluding tests and `styles.css`, per-test coverage, incremental) on the extracted modules, not all of `App.tsx` at once. Add a test for each surviving mutant that is a real gap in conditionals, string literals or arithmetic. Ignore survivors in class names, `aria-*` strings and style code. Target about 80% on logic modules. Stryker support for the repo's vitest version is unverified; the plan's fallback is a hand-picked list of manual mutations.

For new-behaviour mode, suggest implementing one scenario at a time with outside-in TDD, starting with the walking-skeleton scenario.

Suggest an independent review with the `bdd-reviewer` agent (skill `review-bdd-scenarios`) before implementation or refactoring starts, if those exist in this repo.

## Anti-patterns to refuse

- Scenarios written from the code structure instead of the operator's goal.
- Test-per-function or test-per-branch scenarios.
- Imperative click-by-click scenarios.
- Assertions on markup, CSS classes, `aria-*` strings, component state or storage.
- Tests that import or mock `api.ts`, `config.ts` or other internals.
- `let`/`beforeEach` shared state; real timers; real network.
- Fixing a quirk inside a characterisation suite.
- A huge Background, or Scenario Outlines whose rows exercise different rules.
- Writing tests before the user has seen the scenarios.

---
name: write-bdd-scenarios
description: Discover and write high-quality Gherkin scenarios in features/*.feature and derive skipped Playwright component tests in src/*.ct.tsx from them, ready for outside-in TDD with red-green-step. Use when asked to specify, plan, or write the next feature, scenarios, acceptance criteria, or BDD tests.
---

# Write BDD scenarios

Turn a feature idea into a Gherkin spec and a matching set of skipped acceptance tests. Implementation is out of scope: hand off to `red-green-step`.

The reasoning and sources behind each rule are in [references/sources.md](references/sources.md). Read it when a rule needs justifying or you are unsure how to apply one.

## 1. Understand before writing

BDD is a conversation first and a file second. Do not jump to scenarios.

- Read `features/*.feature`, `src/*.ct.tsx` and `src/App.tsx` so the new work reuses the existing vocabulary and does not duplicate scenarios.
- State the story: "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [value]." If you cannot name the value, ask the user. A story with no value is a candidate to drop.
- Run an Example Mapping pass in text, then show it to the user before writing files:
  - **Rules**: the acceptance criteria, one line each.
  - **Examples**: concrete cases under each rule, using real values ("Coffee", "4.50"), not "valid input".
  - **Questions**: anything you cannot answer from the repo or the story.
- Probe each rule with Liz Keogh's two questions:
  - Context: is there another context in which the same event gives a different outcome? (empty list, zero, duplicates, whitespace, very large values, decimals)
  - Outcome: is there another outcome that matters? (what the form shows afterwards, what is kept, what is not changed)
- Ask the user about the open questions with `AskUserQuestion`. Do not invent business rules. Stories discovered along the way that are out of scope go in a "Not now" list, not in the feature.
- Too many rules or examples means the story is too big. Propose a split.

## 2. Write the feature file

Location and naming come from CLAUDE.md: `features/<kebab-case-feature>.feature`.

Structure:

- `Feature:` title, then the story in the three-line "As a / I want / So that" form.
- `Background:` only for context every scenario needs, at most 4 lines.
- `Rule:` blocks when a feature has several distinct business rules, each grouping the examples that illustrate it.
- `Scenario:` for each example. Use `Scenario Outline` with `Examples` only when rows differ by data alone and the same outcome shape holds.

Rules for every scenario:

1. **One behaviour per scenario.** One When, and Then steps that all describe the same outcome.
2. **3-5 steps.** Longer means it is testing more than one thing or leaking mechanics.
3. **Declarative, not imperative.** Describe what the user achieves, not keystrokes. Apply Cucumber's test: would the wording change if the UI changed? If yes, rewrite it. "When I add an expense named "Coffee" with amount "5"" beats three steps filling fields and clicking.
4. **Not too declarative either.** Keep the vocabulary the UI contract needs (the "Name" and "Amount" fields, the "Add" button, expense rows, error text) so a test can be derived. Where a precise UI fact is the behaviour itself, as with "the name field is empty", state it.
5. **Concrete values.** Use realistic data that makes the rule visible. Pick values on both sides of every boundary.
6. **Context, event, outcome.** Given is a state, When is one event, Then is an observable result. Never put an action in Then, never put an assertion in Given.
7. **Observable outcomes only.** Then steps describe what the user sees, not internal state, function calls or storage.
8. **Atomic steps.** No conjunction steps such as "Given I have a Coffee and a Groceries expense". Split into `And` steps.
9. **Titles state the rule.** "Cannot add an expense without a name", not "Test 3" or "Validation".
10. **Domain language.** Use the words the user would use. Reuse existing phrasing from `features/` so steps stay consistent. No technical terms such as "state", "component" or "DOM".
11. **Independent scenarios.** None may rely on another scenario having run.
12. **No coupled scenarios.** If one scenario is necessarily true whenever another one is, merge them or drop the weaker one. The `red-green-step` skill stops on this, so catch it here.

Order scenarios from the walking skeleton outwards: the simplest end-to-end happy path first, then variations, then edge cases and errors. This order is the order of the TDD steps.

## 3. Review before showing the user

Check each scenario against the list below and fix failures silently:

- Does it have a business reason to exist, not just a code path to cover?
- Could a non-programmer read it and say whether it is right?
- Is any step a UI mechanic that belongs in the test code instead?
- Does any pair of scenarios pass or fail together?
- Is there a missing context or outcome from the Keogh questions?

Then present the feature file and the list of open questions or "Not now" items. Wait for the user's approval before deriving tests.

## 4. Derive the acceptance tests

After approval, write one Playwright component test per scenario. Follow the "Playwright component tests" section of CLAUDE.md exactly (file naming, locators, timeouts, one test per Scenario or Examples row). In addition:

- Mount `<App />` and drive only the public surface: labels, roles and visible text. No component internals, no mocks of the app's own code.
- Name each test after its scenario title, in plain words.
- Put the three Gherkin phases in the test body in order, with a blank line before the assertion: setup, action, assertion. Do not add comments.
- Extract the existing small helpers (field locators, `addExpense`, `expectExpenseRow`) and add new ones for new domain phrases, so a test reads like its scenario. Reuse helpers that already exist in the file.
- Each test builds its own data inline. Share nothing mutable between tests.
- Write every new test as `test.skip(`. The only exception is when the user says to start with the first one.
- Run `npx tsc -b` and `npm run lint`. The tests must compile and mount. Running `npm run test:ct` needs the sandbox disabled, see `red-green-step`.

## 5. Hand off to outside-in TDD

Finish by reporting:

- the scenarios written, grouped by rule, in implementation order
- the open questions and "Not now" items
- the first test to drive, which should be the walking-skeleton scenario

Before any implementation, suggest an independent review of the result with the `bdd-reviewer` agent (skill `review-bdd-scenarios`). Fix its blocking findings first.

Then suggest running `red-green-step`, or the `red-green-implementer` agent, one scenario at a time. Do not write production code in this skill. A scenario must fail for a missing behaviour before anyone implements it.

## Anti-patterns to refuse

- Scenarios written from the code instead of from the user's goal.
- Test-per-function or test-per-branch scenarios.
- Imperative click-by-click scenarios.
- Scenarios asserting implementation details (CSS classes, state, storage).
- A huge Background.
- Scenario Outlines whose rows exercise different rules.
- Writing tests before the user has seen the scenarios.

# Sources and rationale

Material behind the `write-bdd-scenarios` skill. Each entry says what was taken from the source and where it shows up in the skill. Pages marked "fetched" were read directly while building the skill. Pages marked "not read" were only seen in search results, so check them before quoting them.

## Behaviour-driven development

### Dan North, "Introducing BDD" (fetched)
https://dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/

- Think in behaviours, not tests. One behaviour is one sentence. Taken into: scenario rule 1 and titles stating the rule.
- Name behaviours as sentences. "Should" invites you to challenge the premise. Taken into: test names in plain words.
- Pick the next behaviour by asking "what is the next most important thing the system doesn't do?" Taken into: ordering scenarios by value, walking skeleton first.
- A story's acceptance criteria are its behaviour, written as Given / When / Then. Taken into: step 1 and step 2.
- Story form "As a / I want / So that" forces a value clause. Taken into: step 1.
- Share one vocabulary between business and developers. Taken into: scenario rule 10.

### Martin Fowler, "GivenWhenThen" (fetched)
https://martinfowler.com/bliki/GivenWhenThen.html

- Given is the state before, When is the behaviour, Then is the expected change. Then should only query state. Taken into: scenario rule 6 and 7.
- Same shape as Arrange, Act, Assert. Taken into: test body layout in step 4.

### Liz Keogh (partly fetched)
- Conversational patterns (fetched): https://lizkeogh.com/2011/09/22/conversational-patterns-in-bdd/ . Context questioning and outcome questioning. Taken into: step 1 probing questions and the review checklist.
- "Given, When, Then - the only way?" (search result only, not read): https://lizkeogh.com/2008/01/28/given-when-then-the-only-way/ . Concrete examples matter more than the template. Taken into: the principle that the conversation comes before the file.
- "Real conversations in BDD", Oredev 2015 (search result only, not read): https://vimeo.com/144723689 . Examples as the way to have the conversation.

### Gojko Adzic, "Specification by Example" (search results only, not read)
https://www.infoq.com/articles/specification-by-example-book

- Derive scope from goals, illustrate with examples, refine the specification, automate validation, validate frequently, evolve into living documentation. Taken into: the overall flow, and the reason scenarios must stay readable by non-programmers.

### Matt Wynne, Example Mapping (fetched)
https://cucumber.io/docs/bdd/example-mapping/

- Story, rules, examples, questions. Taken into: step 1. Red questions go to the user, they are not guessed.

## Gherkin

### Cucumber, "Better Gherkin" (fetched)
https://cucumber.io/docs/bdd/better-gherkin/

- Describe intended behaviour, not implementation. The rewrite test: would the wording change if the implementation changed? Taken into: scenario rule 3.
- Declarative scenarios stay valid when the UI or mechanism changes. Imperative ones can be right in some contexts. Taken into: rules 3 and 4, where the project's UI contract limits how abstract steps can get.
- Named personas beat "User A". Not adopted: this app has a single user, so the skill uses concrete values instead.

### Cucumber, Gherkin reference (fetched)
https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference/

- Rule groups scenarios by business rule. Background is short, at most about 4 lines. Examples recommended at 3-5 steps. Scenario Outline rows are runs of one template. Taken into: step 2 structure.

### Cucumber, anti-patterns (fetched)
https://cucumber.io/docs/guides/anti-patterns/

- Feature-coupled steps and conjunction steps. Taken into: scenario rule 8. In this repo steps are not bound to step definitions, so only the conjunction rule applies.

### Community guides (search results only, not read)
- https://automationpanda.com/2017/01/26/bdd-101-the-gherkin-language/
- https://github.com/andredesousa/gherkin-best-practices
- https://selleo.com/blog/how-to-start-writing-gherkin-test-scenarios . Warns against ultra-declarative steps too vague to automate. Taken into: scenario rule 4.

- Chapter 5, "Start Each Feature with an Acceptance Test" and "Separate Tests That Measure Progress from Those That Catch Regressions": a failing acceptance test drives the feature, and finished ones become regression tests. - Chapter 5, "Develop from the Inputs to the Outputs": acceptance tests go through the system's outer surface. Taken into: step 4, mount `<App />`, drive only labels, roles and text.

I rewrote `.claude/skills/write-bdd-scenarios/SKILL.md` and added a section to `references/sources.md` so the skill follows the framework in the plan. Nothing has been run or tested. The skill was written for a different app (an expense tracker with Playwright component tests), so most of the test-writing steps were replaced.

**What changed**
- **Target:** scenarios go in `apps/user-ui/features/<area>.feature`. Tests go in `apps/user-ui/src/characterisation/<area>.test.tsx`, one file per area from the plan (auth, sidebar, timeline and so on). The plan doesn't name these paths, so I chose them. Tell me if you want different ones.
- **Test stack:** the skill now says to mount the real `<App />` with `happy-dom` and Testing Library, a hand-rolled `fetch` route table, a fake `WebSocket` and fake timers. Tests may import only `App`, `types.ts`, the harness and factories. They must not import or mock `api.ts` or `config.ts`.
- **What a scenario may assert:** what the operator sees, plus the HTTP requests the app sends (method, URL, body). Class names, `aria-*` strings and internal state are not allowed. Transport and time conditions such as "the realtime connection is down" or "10 seconds pass" must be visible Given/When steps.
- **Two modes:**
  - Characterisation is the default. Scenarios describe what the app does today, tests are active, and they pass on first write.
  - New behaviour keeps the old `it.skip` and one-test-at-a-time flow.
- **Quirks:** odd current behaviour (such as the unlisted `DIRECT_GROUP` channels) is pinned as it is, tagged `@quirk` and logged for a separate fix ticket. It is never fixed inside a characterisation suite.
- **Hand-off:** instead of `red-green-step`, the skill now reports timing against the 10s suite and 200ms per-test budget. It then follows plan step 0c: Stryker on the extracted modules, a test for each real surviving mutant, about 80% as the target.

**Things to check**
- The skill refers to a shared harness (fetch stub, fake `WebSocket`, `renderApp`) in `apps/user-ui/src/characterisation/`. Plan step 0a covers tooling but doesn't name that module, so the skill creates it as the first commit if it's missing.
- The `bdd-reviewer` agent and `review-bdd-scenarios` skill that the old skill pointed to aren't in my agent list. I kept the reference but made it conditional on them existing.
- The Feathers and Stryker notes in `sources.md` are from memory, not fetched, and the file says so.

Turn an area of observable `apps/user-ui` behaviour into a Vitest suite that mounts the real `<App />`. There are no `.feature` files: the test is the specification. - **New behaviour.** Tests describe something the app does not do yet. Write them as `it.skip(` and hand them to TDD one at a time.

The reasoning behind the rules is in [references/sources.md](references/sources.md).

## 1. Understand before writing

BDD is a conversation first and a file second. Do not jump to tests.

- Read the plan's "Behaviours to pin" list, existing `apps/user-ui/src/characterisation/*.test.tsx` and the code for the area (`apps/user-ui/src/App.tsx` and neighbours), plus `docs/SPEC.md`. Reuse existing helpers and vocabulary and do not duplicate tests.
- State the story: "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [value]." If you cannot name the value, ask the user.
- Run an Example Mapping pass in text and show it to the user before writing the file:
  - **Rules**: one line each.
  - **Examples**: concrete cases per rule with real values ("#general", "Direct: alice, bob", "Load previous messages"). Each example becomes one test.
  - **Questions**: anything you cannot answer from the repo.
- Probe each rule with Liz Keogh's two questions:
  - Context: is there another context where the same event gives a different outcome? (archived, read-only, private vs public vs team-shared, offline agent, WebSocket down)
  - Outcome: is there another outcome that matters? (what is shown, kept or hidden afterwards, which request is sent)
- Ask the user the open questions with `AskUserQuestion`. Do not invent business rules.
- **Quirks.** In characterisation mode, pin code that looks wrong as it is and log it in a "Quirks" list. Do not fix it and do not skip it. Example from the plan: `DIRECT_GROUP` and `AGENT_AGENT_DM` channels pass the visibility rule but match no sidebar group, so they are never listed. Put `[quirk]` at the start of the test name so it is easy to find for the separate fix ticket.
- Out-of-scope behaviours go in a "Not now" list.
- Too many rules or examples means the area is too big. Propose a split. Areas follow the plan: auth, workspace load, sidebar, timeline, loading, composer, dialogs and management. One test file per area.

Wait for the user's approval of the example map, then write the tests.

## 2. Write the tests

File: `apps/user-ui/src/characterisation/<area>.test.tsx`. Follow the plan's approach exactly.

**Stack**

- Vitest with `happy-dom` (switch a single file to `jsdom` only if a behaviour needs it) and Testing Library. `fireEvent` for plain state changes; `user-event` only where realistic typing matters (Enter vs Shift+Enter, IME composition).
- Mount the real `<App />`. Fake only the outside world: a hand-rolled `fetch` stub with a route table, a fake `WebSocket` class the test can push events through, and the browser APIs (`history`/`location`, `clipboard`, `window.confirm`, `requestAnimationFrame`, fake timers). Stub `scrollHeight` and similar layout properties where needed and accept partial coverage there.
- Use the shared harness (fetch stub, fake WebSocket, `renderApp`) from `apps/user-ui/src/characterisation/`. If it does not exist yet, create it first, as its own commit (plan step 0a).

**What tests may import**

- Only `App`, types from `types.ts`, the harness, and factory functions (`getMockChannel`, `getMockEvent`, ...). Never import or mock `api.ts`, `config.ts` or any other internal module, or moving them would force test edits.
- Factories return complete objects with `Partial<T>` overrides. Keep fixtures small (for example 3 channels). No `let`, no `beforeEach`. Each test builds its own data and renders a fresh `App`.

**Naming and layout**

- Group tests in `describe` blocks by rule. Name each test after the behaviour as a plain sentence that states the rule ("shows an error for wrong credentials"), not "test 3" or "validation".
- Context, event, outcome in order, with a blank line before the assertion. No comments.
- One behaviour per test: one action, and assertions that all describe the same outcome.
- Concrete values on both sides of each boundary (7 vs 8 password characters, one channel vs none).
- Extract helpers for domain phrases ("signInAs", "openChannel", "receiveEvent") so a test reads like a sentence. Reuse existing ones.
- Tests are independent. None relies on another having run.
- If one test is necessarily true whenever another is, merge them or drop the weaker one.

**What to assert**

- Two things are observable: what the operator sees (visible text and roles), and the HTTP requests the app sends (method, URL, body), since that is its real contract with the API.
- Never assert internal state, hooks, module calls, storage, class names, `aria-*` strings or layout. The plan treats those as implementation detail.

**Time**

- Fake timers everywhere. Advance the fake clock and flush promises. No real `waitFor` timeouts. Conditions like "realtime connection is down" or "10 seconds pass" are explicit setup or action lines in the test.

**Speed budget**

- Whole suite under about 10 seconds, any single test under about 200ms. After writing a suite, run `npx vitest run apps/user-ui --reporter=verbose` and fix anything over budget immediately.

**Modes**

- Characterisation: tests are active and must be green.
- New behaviour: write every test as `it.skip(`.

**Checks**

- `npm run lint` and `npm test` stay green. Do not edit `App.tsx` while writing characterisation tests (plan step 0).

## 3. Review before showing the user

Fix failures silently:

- Does each test have a business reason to exist, not just a branch to cover?
- Could someone who has not read the code tell from the test name and body whether the behaviour is right?
- Does any pair of tests pass or fail together?
- Is a missing context or outcome from the Keogh questions covered?
- Is any assertion on markup? Remove it.
- Does it import an internal module? Remove it.

## 4. Mutation check and hand-off

In characterisation mode, report:

- the tests written, grouped by rule
- the quirks pinned, for separate fix tickets
- the open questions and "Not now" items
- suite timing against the budget

Then follow plan step 0c: run Stryker (vitest runner, scope `apps/user-ui/src/**`, excluding tests and `styles.css`, per-test coverage, incremental) on the extracted modules, not on all of `App.tsx` at once. Add a test for each surviving mutant that is a real gap in conditionals, string literals or arithmetic. Ignore survivors in class names, `aria-*` strings and style code. - Tests written from the code structure instead of the operator's goal.
- Test-per-function or test-per-branch tests.
- Assertions on markup, CSS classes, `aria-*` strings, component state or storage.
- Tests that import or mock `api.ts`, `config.ts` or other internals.
- `let`/`beforeEach` shared state; real timers; real network.
- Fixing a quirk inside a characterisation suite.
- Writing tests before the user has seen the example map.

# Sources and rationale

Material behind the `write-bdd-scenarios` skill. Each entry says what was taken from the source and where it shows up in the skill. Pages marked "fetched" were read directly while building the skill. Pages marked "not read" were only seen in search results, so check them before quoting them.

## Behaviour-driven development

### Dan North, "Introducing BDD" (fetched)
https://dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/

- Think in behaviours, not tests. One behaviour is one sentence. Taken into: scenario rule 1 and titles stating the rule.
- Name behaviours as sentences. "Should" invites you to challenge the premise. Taken into: test names in plain words.
- Pick the next behaviour by asking "what is the next most important thing the system doesn't do?" Taken into: ordering scenarios by value, walking skeleton first.
- A story's acceptance criteria are its behaviour, written as Given / When / Then. Taken into: step 1 and step 2.
- Story form "As a / I want / So that" forces a value clause. Taken into: step 1.
- Share one vocabulary between business and developers. Taken into: scenario rule 10.

### Martin Fowler, "GivenWhenThen" (fetched)
https://martinfowler.com/bliki/GivenWhenThen.html

- Given is the state before, When is the behaviour, Then is the expected change. Then should only query state. Taken into: scenario rule 6 and 7.
- Same shape as Arrange, Act, Assert. Taken into: test body layout in step 4.

### Liz Keogh (partly fetched)
- Conversational patterns (fetched): https://lizkeogh.com/2011/09/22/conversational-patterns-in-bdd/ . Context questioning and outcome questioning. Taken into: step 1 probing questions and the review checklist.
- "Given, When, Then - the only way?" (search result only, not read): https://lizkeogh.com/2008/01/28/given-when-then-the-only-way/ . Concrete examples matter more than the template. Taken into: the principle that the conversation comes before the file.
- "Real conversations in BDD", Oredev 2015 (search result only, not read): https://vimeo.com/144723689 . Examples as the way to have the conversation.

### Gojko Adzic, "Specification by Example" (search results only, not read)
https://www.infoq.com/articles/specification-by-example-book

- Derive scope from goals, illustrate with examples, refine the specification, automate validation, validate frequently, evolve into living documentation. Taken into: the overall flow, and the reason scenarios must stay readable by non-programmers.

### Matt Wynne, Example Mapping (fetched)
https://cucumber.io/docs/bdd/example-mapping/

- Story, rules, examples, questions. Taken into: step 1. Red questions go to the user, they are not guessed.

## Gherkin

### Cucumber, "Better Gherkin" (fetched)
https://cucumber.io/docs/bdd/better-gherkin/

- Describe intended behaviour, not implementation. The rewrite test: would the wording change if the implementation changed? Taken into: scenario rule 3.
- Declarative scenarios stay valid when the UI or mechanism changes. Imperative ones can be right in some contexts. Taken into: rules 3 and 4, where the project's UI contract limits how abstract steps can get.
- Named personas beat "User A". Not adopted: this app has a single user, so the skill uses concrete values instead.

### Cucumber, Gherkin reference (fetched)
https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference/

- Rule groups scenarios by business rule. Background is short, at most about 4 lines. Examples recommended at 3-5 steps. Scenario Outline rows are runs of one template. Taken into: step 2 structure.

### Cucumber, anti-patterns (fetched)
https://cucumber.io/docs/guides/anti-patterns/

- Feature-coupled steps and conjunction steps. Taken into: scenario rule 8. In this repo steps are not bound to step definitions, so only the conjunction rule applies.

### Community guides (search results only, not read)
- https://automationpanda.com/2017/01/26/bdd-101-the-gherkin-language/
- https://github.com/andredesousa/gherkin-best-practices
- https://selleo.com/blog/how-to-start-writing-gherkin-test-scenarios . Warns against ultra-declarative steps too vague to automate. Taken into: scenario rule 4.

Treat numeric limits from these as opinion.

## Outside-in TDD

### Steve Freeman and Nat Pryce, "Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests" (table of contents fetched, text not read)
https://growing-object-oriented-software.com/toc.html

- Chapter 4, "First, Test a Walking Skeleton": the thinnest end-to-end slice first. Taken into: step 2 ordering and step 5 hand-off.
- Chapter 5, "Start Each Feature with an Acceptance Test" and "Separate Tests That Measure Progress from Those That Catch Regressions": a failing acceptance test drives the feature, and finished ones become regression tests. Taken into: why tests are written skipped and unskipped one at a time in `red-green-step`.
- Chapter 5, "Write the Test That You'd Want to Read" and Chapter 21, "Test Readability": tests as specification. Taken into: step 4 helper extraction.
- Chapter 5, "Develop from the Inputs to the Outputs": acceptance tests go through the system's outer surface. Taken into: step 4, mount `<App />`, drive only labels, roles and text.

## Characterisation tests and mutation testing

Not fetched; from general knowledge, check before quoting.

- Michael Feathers, "Working Effectively with Legacy Code": characterisation tests pin what code does today, not what it should do, so it can be changed safely. Taken into: the default mode, and logging quirks instead of fixing them.
- Stryker (vitest runner): mutation testing as the check that a test passing on first write would still catch a break. Taken into: step 5 and the 80% target. Compatibility with the repo's vitest version is unverified, as the plan says.

## How the sources map onto this repo

- The framework itself (happy-dom, hand-rolled fetch stub, fake WebSocket, fake timers, factories, no `let`/`beforeEach`, suites per area, speed budget) comes from `docs/1-refactoring-1-user-ui-refactoring-plan.md`, not from the sources above.
- The tests mount the whole app, so they are outside-in tests at the UI boundary. Inner unit-level tests, when needed, come from the TDD workflow in `~/.claude/docs/workflow.md`, and are not written by this skill.
- Characterisation tests pass on first write by design, so the one-at-a-time RED-GREEN cycle applies only to the new-behaviour mode, where tests are written as `it.skip`.

message.content: okay, what's the plan for writing characterization tests you're going to follow

content.text:
Here is the plan I'd follow. It comes from step 0 of `docs/1-refactoring-1-user-ui-refactoring-plan.md` and the updated skill. `App.tsx` stays untouched throughout.

**0a. Tooling and harness (one commit, no behaviour tests yet)**
- Add `happy-dom`, Testing Library and a vitest setup for `apps/user-ui`. Root `vitest` only runs node tests today, so the DOM environment has to be scoped to user-ui.
- Build the shared harness in `apps/user-ui/src/characterisation/`:
  - a `fetch` stub with a route table that records requests;
  - a fake `WebSocket` the test can push events through;
  - browser fakes for `history`/`location`, `clipboard`, `confirm`, `requestAnimationFrame` and fake timers;
  - `renderApp` and the factories (`getMockChannel`, `getMockEvent`, ...).
- Write one smoke test (the app mounts and shows the login form) to prove the harness works, and check its timing.

**0b. One suite per area, one commit each**

The order starts with the least coupled areas and ends with the most coupled:
1. auth (session check, login error, forced password change, sign-out);
2. workspace load (`?share=`, `?channel=`, first-channel fallback, archived expansion);
3. sidebar (visibility rules, grouping, search, unread badges, display names);
4. timeline (message vs trace, failure classification, attachments, sensitive reveal, thinking/offline hints);
5. loading and realtime (pagination, merge and dedupe, polling only while the socket is down, reconnect backoff, topic subscribe/unsubscribe);
6. composer (Enter vs Shift+Enter, disabled states, uploads, paste image);
7. dialogs and management (Cmd+K, DM vs channel creation, manage channel, participants, shares, share link).

For each area:
- Do an Example Mapping pass in text first (rules, concrete examples, questions) and get your approval before writing the file.
- Read the code for that area so I pin what it does today.
- Write one test per example against the real `<App />`. Tests assert visible text and the requests sent, and nothing about markup.
- Keep `lint` and `test` green, and run with `--reporter=verbose` to check the 10s suite and 200ms per-test budget.
- Log any odd behaviour as a `[quirk]` test and a note, without fixing it.

**0c. Mutation check**
- Run a spike first to see if Stryker's vitest runner works with the repo's vitest 5.x. If not, fall back to a hand-picked list of manual mutations.
- Run it on a few extracted or isolated logic areas, not all of `App.tsx` at once.
- Add tests for survivors that point at real gaps in conditionals, strings or arithmetic. Ignore survivors in class names, `aria-*` and style code. Target about 80% on logic.
- Refactoring step 1 doesn't start until this is done.

**Known limits**
- Characterisation tests pass on first write, so mutation testing is what shows they would catch a break.
- `happy-dom` has no layout, so scroll and autosize behaviour, such as "New messages below", is only partly testable.
- Effect-ordering and render-time-closure bugs in `loadShell` and `loadMessageNotifications` need explicit tests, because the plan lists them as pitfalls.

Say the word and I'll start with 0a, or tell me if you'd rather reorder the areas.
